topic.subject: social
topic.title: Drainage: rivers of India
topic.scope: Himalayan and peninsular rivers, drainage basins, Ganga and Brahmaputra systems, lakes, river pollution

misconceptions.statement: Himalayan rivers are perennial only because of heavy rainfall.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the source of water with seasonal monsoon patterns.
misconceptions.fix: Himalayan rivers are perennial because they are fed by both melting glaciers and seasonal rainfall.

probe.question: Why do Himalayan rivers flow even in the dry season?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it rains heavily throughout the year in the mountains.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: All rivers in India flow from North to South.
misconceptions.why: Students generalize the flow of the Ganga to the entire country.
misconceptions.fix: Peninsular rivers flow according to the slope of the plateau; many flow from West to East, and some like Narmada flow West.

probe.question: In which direction does the Narmada river flow?
probe.wrong_answer: Southwards towards the Bay of Bengal.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one example works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: A drainage basin is just the river channel itself.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the river path with the entire area that drains into it.
misconceptions.fix: A drainage basin is the entire area of land where water collects and drains into a common outlet like a river or lake.

probe.question: What constitutes a drainage basin?
probe.wrong_answer: The main river channel and its immediate banks.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: River pollution is only caused by industrial waste.
misconceptions.why: Media focus on industrial dumping overshadows domestic and agricultural sources.
misconceptions.fix: Pollution is caused by industrial waste, untreated domestic sewage, and agricultural runoff containing fertilizers.

probe.question: What are the primary causes of river pollution?
probe.wrong_answer: Only factories dumping chemicals into the water.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Himalayan rivers like the Ganga and Indus start in the plains and flow upward into the mountains.
misconceptions.why: Students see the large, wide river in the plains and assume that is where the river begins.
misconceptions.fix: Himalayan rivers originate in the mountains (e.g. Gangotri glacier, Mansarovar region), cut gorges and carry water and sediments down to the plains.

probe.question: Where does the River Ganga (as Bhagirathi) originate?
probe.wrong_answer: In the Ganga plains near Allahabad, then it flows towards the mountains.

misconceptions.root_belief: Rivers begin where they are largest

misconceptions.statement: Peninsular rivers are older and carry more water than Himalayan rivers because they are in the oldest part of India.
misconceptions.why: Students link age of landmass with size and volume of rivers.
misconceptions.fix: Peninsular rivers are seasonal, depend on rainfall, and have smaller basins and less water; they are older and have graded, shallow valleys, but Himalayan rivers are larger and perennial.

probe.question: Which has more water throughout the year: the Krishna or the Ganga?
probe.wrong_answer: The Krishna, because Peninsular rivers are older and bigger.

misconceptions.statement: The Ganga is formed only by the Alaknanda river.
misconceptions.why: Students remember one headstream and ignore the Bhagirathi and the confluence at Devprayag.
misconceptions.fix: The Ganga is formed at Devprayag where the Alaknanda and the Bhagirathi meet; it is then joined by Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi and others.

probe.question: Name the two streams that join at Devprayag to form the Ganga.

misconceptions.root_belief: A river has one single source stream
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Class 9 Geography chapter 3 error analysis

misconceptions.statement: The Brahmaputra is called by the same name and carries little water throughout its entire course in India.
misconceptions.why: Students think a river keeps one name and one nature from source to mouth.
misconceptions.fix: The Brahmaputra rises in Tibet as the Tsangpo, is called Dihang in Arunachal Pradesh and Brahmaputra in Assam, and carries huge water volume and silt, often causing floods in Assam.

probe.question: What is the Brahmaputra called in Tibet?

misconceptions.statement: The Narmada and Tapi flow east into the Bay of Bengal like most Peninsular rivers.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralise that most Peninsular rivers are east-flowing and forget the rift valleys.
misconceptions.fix: Narmada and Tapi flow west through rift valleys and drain into the Arabian Sea, forming estuaries instead of deltas.

probe.question: Into which water body does the Narmada drain?

misconceptions.statement: East-flowing rivers like the Mahanadi and Krishna form estuaries, not deltas.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up which coast gets deltas and which gets estuaries.
misconceptions.fix: East-flowing rivers form large deltas on the east coast (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri); west-flowing rivers form estuaries.

probe.question: What landform does the Godavari form at its mouth?

misconceptions.statement: All lakes in India are freshwater lakes formed by rivers.
misconceptions.why: Students think lakes are always freshwater and river-made.
misconceptions.fix: Lakes may be freshwater or salt water (Sambhar is salt; Chilika is a lagoon), and form by glaciers, tectonic activity, wind, rivers or humans (Dal, Wular, ox-bow).

probe.question: Is Sambhar Lake a freshwater lake?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all lakes in India are freshwater.

misconceptions.statement: A water divide is a dam or wall built to separate river waters.
misconceptions.why: Students link 'divide' with a human-made barrier.
misconceptions.fix: A water divide is a natural upland, such as a mountain or ridge, that separates two neighbouring drainage basins.

probe.question: What is a water divide?
probe.wrong_answer: A dam built across a river to divide its water.
